panels.title: Leg latency — avg: discovery / quote / transfer
panels.description: How much time is spent in each phase — discovery (party lookup), quote, and transfer. Means are additive across stages (unlike the p50/p95/p99 panels below), so this is also the reference line every composition/hop-breakdown panel in the sections below is measured against.

Leg latency — p95: discovery / quote / transfer
Leg latency — p99: discovery / quote / transfer
panels.description: Duplicates the phase-p99 panel on the k6 dashboard, kept here too so this dashboard is self-contained for a full leg breakdown.

panels.title: Discovery leg — payer FSP -> switch -> payee FSP -> back (mean)
panels.description: Full physical-path walk of the discovery round trip, mean per hop. Payer FSP's GET /parties enters the switch (1); the ALS GET handler runs (2), resolving the payee's DFSP - served from the ALS participant cache on ~84% of lookups, the rest a real GET to the msisdn-oracle (3, shown amortized per lookup: the call itself is ~3 ms but fires on only ~16% of lookups); the switch forwards the lookup to the payee (4); the payee's own round trip (5); the payee's PUT /parties callback lands back on the switch (6), the ALS PUT handler processes it (7) and the switch relays it to the payer (8) - whose arrival releases the payer sim's HTTP response that k6 is timing. Hops 4 and 8 share one Istio label (account-lookup-service to sim), split by destination: this campaign's payers are the odd-numbered sims (fsp201/203/205/207), payees the even (fsp202/204/206/208). Not shown: the payer sim's own processing of hop 8, and the per-lookup cache reads (getParticipant/getEndpoint) which are in the internal-steps panel below - both fall into the inter-stage remainder in the composition panel.

panels.title: Discovery leg — switch-side internal steps (mean)
panels.description: What line 2 ('switch: ALS handler') on the panel above is actually made of, plus the switch-side step that processes the payee's callback (which that panel's line 5 hands off to). Ordered roughly as the code executes: GET ingress -> participant-endpoint cache lookup -> participant registry lookup(s) -> the outbound oracle/DFSP call -> PUT ingress handling the callback. getEndpoint/getParticipant near zero means the participant cache is doing its job; fetchParticipant/fetchParticipants and sendRequest carry the real internal cost.

panels.title: Discovery leg composition (mean): handler time vs. inter-stage
panels.description: ALS ingress handler mean vs. everything else in the discovery leg (oracle lookup, Kafka-adjacent hops, DFSP round trip).

panels.title: Quote leg — payer FSP -> switch -> payee FSP -> back (mean)
panels.description: Full physical-path walk of the quote round trip, mean per hop. Payer FSP's POST /quotes enters the switch (1); the quotes-post handler validates it (2) and the quoting-service-handler forwards it to the payee (3); the payee's own round trip incl. its backend call (4); the payee's PUT /quotes callback lands back on the switch (5), the quotes-put handler processes it (6) and the quoting-service-handler relays it to the payer (7) - whose arrival releases the payer sim's HTTP response that k6 is timing. Hops 3 and 7 share one Istio label (quoting-service-handler to sim), split by destination: this campaign's payers are the odd-numbered sims (fsp201/203/205/207), payees the even (fsp202/204/206/208). Quoting runs SIMPLE_ROUTING_MODE (no persistence), so hops 2 and 6 are sub-millisecond; the bulk of the leg is the two Kafka hops (its own panel) and hop 4. Not shown: the payer sim's own processing of hop 7 - it falls into the inter-stage remainder in the composition panel below.

panels.title: Quote leg — switch-side internal steps (mean)
panels.description: What lines 2 and 5 on the panel above are actually made of, in code order: POST ingress -> validate -> handle -> forward-to-payee (line 3's app-level view) -> [payee round trip] -> PUT ingress -> handle-update -> forward-to-payer (also line 3's app-level view, other direction). quoting-service runs SIMPLE_ROUTING_MODE — no DB query anywhere in this leg, moja_model_quote here is application function time, not database time despite the metric name.

panels.title: Quote leg composition (mean): handler time vs. inter-stage
panels.description: quoting-service runs SIMPLE_ROUTING_MODE (validate + forward, no persistence, no DB query) — expect the handler lines near zero and inter-stage to account for almost the entire leg. group-quotes-handler-post/-put export no Kafka lag data in this cluster, so inter-stage can't be broken out into a queueing estimate the way transfer's can below.

panels.title: Transfer leg — payer FSP -> switch -> payee FSP -> back (mean)
panels.description: Full physical-path walk of the transfer round trip, mean per hop, every on-path step. Payer FSP's POST /transfers enters the switch (1); the prepare handler commits it (2), the position-batch handler applies the prepare-side position (3), the notification handler emits the PREPARE event (4) and the switch forwards it to the payee (5); the payee's own round trip incl. its backend call (6); the payee's PUT /transfers fulfil callback lands back on the switch (7), the fulfil handler commits it (8), the position-batch handler applies the fulfil-side position (9), the notification handler emits the COMMIT event (10) and the switch sends it to the payer (11) — whose arrival releases the payer sim's HTTP response that k6 is timing. Hops 3≡9 and 4≡10 by construction: moja_transfer_position_batch and moja_notification_event are not phase-split, so each firing reads the same mean. Hops 5 and 11 share one Istio label (notification-handler → sim), split by destination: this campaign's payers are the odd-numbered sims (fsp201/203/205/207), payees the even (fsp202/204/206/208). Not shown: the payer sim's own processing of hop 11 before it replies to k6 (no DFSP-side reporter=destination series) and the Kafka queueing between every stage (its own panel) — both fall into the inter-stage remainder in the composition panel below.

panels.title: Transfer leg — switch-side internal steps (mean)
panels.description: How much of lines 2 and 6 on the panel above is actually MySQL commit time (prepare/fulfil DB commit — a subset of those handler means, not additional), plus the two off-path switch steps every transfer also pays for: the position-batch commit and the notification fan-out, each firing once on the prepare side and once on the fulfil side (means shown here are per-firing; the composition panel below doubles them to get each one's true contribution to the leg).

panels.title: Transfer leg composition (mean): handler time vs. inter-stage
panels.description: Stacked mean components of the transfer leg. position-batch and notification are each doubled — both fire once on the prepare side and once on the fulfil side per transfer. 'inter-stage' is not a real metric: it's the k6-measured transfer mean minus the four handler means, i.e. time spent queued in Kafka between stages. If this goes negative, a handler mean has drifted above its actual share (check for a metric-name/label mismatch before trusting the other lines).

panels.title: Transfer leg — Kafka inter-stage queueing (estimated: lag / consumption rate)
panels.description: Crude produce-to-consume delay estimate (lag messages / consumption rate) for the three transfer-path topics whose consumer groups actually export lag. topic-transfer-fulfil (cl-group-transfer-fulfil) exports no lag data in this cluster and is missing from this panel entirely — do not read its absence as zero queueing. Assumes roughly steady-state draining; treat as directional, not exact.

panels.title: Transfer leg — wide-span closure
panels.description: tx_transfer_prepare/tx_transfer_fulfil are wide-span app histograms that already CONTAIN every hop in the panels above (including their Kafka inter-stage time) plus their own commit cost — they are not additional legs. Summed with the DFSP round trip that sits between them, this should stack to within a few percent of the k6 transfer mean: the cleanest available proof that the transfer leg is fully accounted for end to end.
